slides.title: Slips, Trips, and Falls
slides.description:
At the end of this training, you will be able to:

Identify 2 requirements of OSHA's walking and working surfaces standard that apply to your workplace.

Identify common causes of slips, trips and falls (STF) within your workplace.

Evaluate your workplace for hazards associated with walking and working surfaces.

Generate ideas on how to control for these identified hazards.

slides.title: Injuries from Slips, Trips and Falls
slides.description:
Common Injuries:

  • Sprains, strains
  • Bruises, contusions
  • Fractures
  • Abrasions, cuts

Common Affected Body Parts

  • Knee, ankle, foot
  • Wrist, elbow
  • Back
  • Shoulder
  • Hip
  • Head

slides.title: Slip, Trip and Fall hazards can occur in virtually every type of workplace.
NIOSH’s Top 10 Hazards
slides.description:
• Contaminants on the Floor
  • Indoor Walking Surface Irregularities
  • Outdoor Walking Surface Irregularities
  • Weather Conditions: Ice and Snow
  • Inadequate Lighting
  • Stairs and Handrails
  • Stepstools and Ladders
  • Tripping Hazards: Clutter, Loose Cords, etc.
  • Improper Use of Floor Mats and Runners
  • Poor Drainage: Pipes and Drains

slides.title: Contaminants on the Floor
slides.description:
See the photos below with fluid on the floor and dry contaminants both make for slippery situations

See the photos below, surfaces that are highly polished such as marble and ceramic tile can be very slippery even dry. Freshly waxed surfaces can be slippery.

Wall-mounted spill pads for use by employees and visitors

Spill pads and umbrella bags for use in building entryway

High visibility caution sign with warning sign on top or a flashing light on top could be used

slides.title: Indoor Walking Surface Irregularities
slides.description: Damaged, warped, buckled, or uneven flooring surfaces inside facilities can cause employees to stumble, trip, slip, or fall.

slides.title: Outdoor Walking Surface Irregularities
slides.description: Poorly maintained, uneven ground, protruding structures, holes, rocks, leaves, and other debris can cause employees and/or Customers to stumble, trip, slip, or fall. Holes in grassy area between a parking lot and building. Stones and debris on walking surfaces in a parking lot . Area of sloped pavement that should be highlighted with Safety Yellow paint.

slides.title: Prevention Solutions
slides.description: Wheelchair accessible curb leading to building entrance is highlighted and the surface is dimpled for better visibility and traction. Highlight or mark slip and trip hazards for better visibility. Always use bright colors usually bright yellow since it is a universal color for hazards.

slides.title: Weather Conditions:  Water, Ice, and Snow
slides.description: Weather conditions can create hazardous situations which is why it is imperative that we keep up with clearing of any water, Ice, snow, or Leaves.

slides.title: Inadequate Lighting
slides.description: Inadequate lighting can occur in many places hallways, garages, store rooms, shops, stairwells. We need to make sure that everyone can see clearly in our work areas so they can identify any potential hazards.

slides.title: Stairs and Handrails
Prevention Solutions
slides.description: There are many different products that can placed on stairs to reduce potential slipping and usually for little money. Should always make sure that rails are secure.

slides.title: Stepstools and Ladders
slides.description: Stepstools and ladders used incorrectly can lead to serious injury should only use them as intended.

slides.title: OSHA Walking and Working Surfaces Standard:  Subpart D 1910.25-26:  Portable Ladders:
slides.description: All ladders must be inspected periodically, kept in good condition at all times, and must be free from sharp edges, splinters, oil grease, or other defects which would affect their use.

slides.title: Tripping Hazards: Clutter, Loose Wires, etc.
slides.description: Clutter can build up in storage areas, work areas, hallways, and walkways potentially leading to an STF incident. Exposed cords on the floor, stretched across walkways, and tangled near work spaces can catch an employee’s foot and lead to a trip and fall incident. Open cabinet, file, or desk drawers can cause a fall.

slides.title: Prevention Solutions
slides.description:
Retractable cord holder

Cords on floor partially secured with cord cover. Cover can extend over the length of the exposed cord.

slides.title: Improper use of floor mats and runners:
slides.description: Mats are used to prevent STFs to provide slip-resistant walking surfaces by absorbing liquid, and by removing dirt, debris, and liquid from shoes. Mats are only effective if properly used and maintained. Old or poorly placed mats can contribute to slips, trips, and falls

slides.title: Prevention Solutions
slides.description: Install slip-resistant floors in high risk areas (entrances, hallways, and highly polished floors).

slides.title: Poor Drainage:  Pipes and Drains
slides.description: Drains and water pipes that are improperly aligned can cause liquid to spill onto walking surfaces, while clogged drains can cause water to back up onto the floor.

slides.title: Human Factors Leading to Slips Trips and Falls
slides.description:
Drains and water pipes that are improperly aligned can cause liquid to spill onto walking surfaces, while clogged drains can cause water to back up onto the floor.

Health and physical condition can impair a person’s vision, judgment, and balance.

Carrying or moving cumbersome objects, or too many objects, that obstruct your view impair your balance and prevent you from holding onto handrails

Inattentive Behavior: walking, distractions (e.g., using cell phone, talking and not watching where you’re going, etc.)

Taking shortcuts; not using walkways or designated, cleared pathways; being in a hurry, rushing around

slides.title: OSHA Walking and Working Surfaces Standard:  Subpart D 1910.22:  Housekeeping
slides.description: Good housekeeping includes picking up, wiping up, and cleaning up. Requires that all places of employment, passageways, storerooms, and service rooms shall be kept clean and orderly and in a sanitary condition.

slides.title: Maintaining Work Areas
slides.description: Aisles and passageways must be kept clear and in good repair and include safe clearances for mechanical equipment and contain no obstructions that could create a hazard.

slides.title: Prevention Strategies
slides.description:
Develop and maintain a written housekeeping program.

The program might ideally describe:

  • How to immediately report STF hazards
  • Where and how cleaning materials and products are stored
  • When to use wet floor signs and barriers and where signs are stored
  • What cleaning methods are appropriate for different areas and surfaces

slides.description:
Examine Employee STF Injuries

STF Checklist

Employee Communication: Training and Involvement

slides.title: Examine Employee STF Injuries
slides.description:
Review OSHA logs for STF incidents

Review incident reports

Check for “hot spots”

Investigate incidents to find the circumstances to see where prevention measures can be implemented.

slides.title: STF Checklist
slides.description:
Check for hazards on a regular basis

Take pictures!

Have a clear reporting procedure to get things addressed

slides.title: Communication:  Training and Involvement
slides.description: All employees are at risk, therefore all employees should be trained on how to recognize STF hazards, and be involved in the development and implementation of prevention strategies.

questions.question: The most common injuries from STFs are sprains, strains, bruises, fractures, abrasions, and cuts.
Inadequate lighting is a major cause of STFs.
Most places of business don’t have to worry about STFs only plants and construction sites.
Ladders are simple tools and do not need to be inspected regularly they either are working or not.
There is a human element to STFs that all employees need to be aware of.
